For papers selected by screening role and period, plus named systems and landmarks, we check the stated assumptions in the full texts, and we assess eleven temporal knowledge representation and reasoning (KRR) formalisms and a learned baseline on nine attack patterns. Some early alert correlators stated clock and delivery assumptions, and forensics measures clock error. Current provenance-based detectors state no clock bound. Four audited papers describe input-ordering conditions or conventions, but none specifies conditions for conclusion validity across a stated class of delivery failures. In the selected provenance-based systems, campaign composition uses system-specific procedures or objectives, learned state, causal graph queries or language models, and beyond CEP-based query systems, we found no temporal rule language or stream reasoner from KRR applied to host audit data. In 28 of 38 audited provenance-era detector papers, capture or stored evidence is trusted or its manipulation is placed out of scope, and none says which conclusions survive deleted, delayed or forged records. Five open challenges follow from these gaps.
item.dc:creator: Rene Heinzl, Markus Nissl

item.title: Can Open Be Too Open? On the Security and Trustworthiness of Fully Transparent LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.35199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. Drawing analogies to other fields such as software security, it is often believed that increasing transparency inherently increases the security and trustworthiness of the LLM. However, we argue that such claims need to be critically re-evaluated in the context of LLMs. In this paper, we analyze the impact of transparency on LLM security and trustworthiness by reviewing the relevant literature. Our core findings are that, due to the limited reproducibility of LLM pipelines, in practice, users cannot verify the correspondence between open weights and the associated open data and pipeline. Thus, in order to trust a model, users still need to trust that developers acted honestly, reducing the benefits over models that provide less "transparency". Moreover, we find that even when LLMs are fully transparent and trusted, this openness can favor adversaries. Open weights in particular, but also open data and pipelines, can increase the success rate of attacks. Although the same mechanisms can be used to improve the model and protect it against attacks, the current lack of robust lightweight mechanisms to patch LLM vulnerabilities limits the benefits of openness at this time. We note that our analysis is based on current LLM capabilities and analysis tools, and that future developments may require a re-evaluation of these points.
item.dc:creator: Sheila Zingg, Florian Tram\`er, Martin Vechev, Srdjan \v{C}apkun

item.title: False-Alarm Improvements and Detection Trade-Offs in QML Intrusion Detection: A Secondary Analysis of the Kaissar Corpus
item.description: arXiv:2610.35235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Published results in quantum machine learning for intrusion detection (QML-IDS) require joint interpretation of false-positive rate (FPR), attack true-positive rate (TPR), and evaluation provenance. We reconstruct operating points in the 25-entry frame selected by Kaissar and colleagues: 21 included articles, 20 identified documentary families, substantive methodological material consulted for 15, and 24 descriptive points from five. In one test-labelled comparison, a quantum support vector machine reduces FPR from 6.875% for random forest to 3.329%, while TPR decreases from 93.955% to 93.682%; both rates improve against three other comparators. In another study, a complete benign row identifies FPR as 12/6000 (0.200%), despite incomplete attack-side allocation that requires additional assumptions for TPR. Normalized matrices identify detection ranges rather than a unique aggregate rate. A uniform provenance rule separates training-described and test-adjusted results from six conditional illustrations whose independence remains unverified. The contribution is a reproducible interpretation of favorable comparisons and detection trade-offs, without converting descriptive results or hypothetical calculations into operational guarantees.
item.dc:creator: Roberto Fern\'andez-Barrios, Iker Pastor-L\'opez, Asier Gonz\'alez-Santocildes, Pablo Garc\'ia Bringas

item.title: Then there is prompt injection, a malicious email, ...: The Wild Wide West of OpenClaw Agentic System Security
item.description: arXiv:2610.35451v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-powered personal assistant frameworks such as OpenClaw combine LLM reasoning, persistent memory, tool invocation, local execution, and web-based workflows. These capabilities enable useful automation, but they also create security risks when untrusted inputs, model reasoning, tools, memory, and deployment configuration interact without explicit trust boundaries. This paper presents an empirical study of reported security concerns in OpenClaw using two complementary data sources: Reddit discussions and security-tagged GitHub issues. We analyze more than 25K Reddit posts from 13 OpenClaw-related subreddits and identify 162 security-relevant posts with 1,787 associated comments. We further collect 358 security-tagged GitHub issues and retain 180 issues describing concrete security concerns. Using qualitative analysis and evidence-grounded CWE mapping, we identify 521 CWE instances across 59 distinct weakness types, concentrated in access-control failures, sensitive-data exposure, injection, and unsafe execution. We also extract 543 practitioner mitigation suggestions and consolidate them into seven recurring strategies. To complement the empirical analysis, we present an evidence-grounded illustrative reconstruction of a representative sensitive-data exposure pathway using dummy secret values. Our findings show that OpenClaw security issues are not isolated implementation bugs; they reflect recurring trust-boundary failures across the agent execution pipeline. We discuss how these weaknesses map to both traditional software-security categories and agent-specific failure mechanisms, and derive implications for safer agentic systems, including explicit trust boundaries, least-privilege tool access, execution containment, runtime oversight, and defense-in-depth deployment.
item.dc:creator: Mostafijur Rahman Akhond, Mahmuda Khatun, Gias Uddin

item.title: PRISMA: Differentially Private Synthetic In-Car Telemetry via Differentiable Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35521v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differentially private synthesis of in-car energy consumption data is challenging because the output is high-dimensional, and known lower bounds show that the privacy-utility trade-off degrades with the square root of the number of output dimensions. However, we observe that the intrinsic dimensionality of in-car energy consumption is much lower than that of the raw trace: given a small set of contextual personal variables-such as start point, end point, the car model, and the driving behavior-the consumption profile can be largely explained by publicly available map data (including elevation) combined with a physical model of vehicle energy use. We exploit this low intrinsic dimensionality in PRISMA, a Privacy-preserving In-car Synthesis and Modelling Algorithm. PRISMA involves three stages: (i) energy consumption traces are encoded into a low-dimensional latent space; (ii) the distribution of latent vectors is synthesized using the differentially private tabular data synthesis algorithm AIM, and (iii) samples drawn from this distribution are decoded back into full energy consumption traces via a differentiable physics-based simulation, a step that consumes no additional privacy budget since it uses only public information. By using a compact, physically-grounded latent representation of the traces, PRISMA significantly reduces the effective output dimension. Our experimental results show that PRISMA achieves for a competitive $\varepsilon = 0.5$ a better data synthesis performance than prior tabular and marginal-based DP synthesis baselines by preserving the diversity of the original power consumption profiles without collapsing to a small set of modes.
item.dc:creator: Kilian Zeiseweis, Nele Sophie Br\"ugge, Marven Kummerfeldt, Ali Raza, Esfandiar Mohammadi

item.title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.35532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unsafe deserialization turns untrusted data into attacker-controlled execution, and a single vulnerability can admit diverse exploit variants that evade defenses tailored to a known exploit. Existing defenses typically operate at a single enforcement point with limited visibility into the full attack. Combining controls across layers offers complementary protection, but coordinating them to preserve legitimate functionality and adapting them to new variants requires substantial expert effort. We propose JANUS, a red-blue adversarial framework for automated cross-layer defense synthesis. Starting from a known exploit, \sys iteratively refines deployment-specific policies in an isolated offline environment. A black-box attacker probes the current policy for exploit variants using only externally observable feedback. The defender summarizes each verified variant into its security-relevant effects, uses counterfactual replay to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement, and jointly selects and scopes controls across layers. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows. We evaluate JANUS on sixteen vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications against gateway, application, system, and cross-layer defenses. JANUS reduces held-out attack success to 6.2%, compared with 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and preserves 98.4% of benign functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 latency increase.
item.dc:creator: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie

item.title: The Agent in the Middle: How AI-Mediated Access Reshapes Web Vulnerability Exploitation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web services increasingly expose backend interfaces that let users delegate tasks to AI agents, which invoke service operations directly without navigating websites. This shift changes how existing Web vulnerabilities can be exploited. We investigate these changes through VELA, an executable benchmark covering 44 vulnerabilities across twelve Web application families. The benchmark preserves vulnerable backends and derives agent-facing interfaces from legitimate workflows. We evaluate three commercial agents across multiple interface configurations, using controlled comparisons to separate interface effects from agent behavior and independent oracles to verify attack outcomes. Our results show that the agent realizes every attack that direct interface invocation realizes in the reference configuration, so exploitability is set mainly by the interface: 91% of vulnerabilities remain exploitable under the reference design. Interface restrictions prevent some attacks by removing required operations or limiting input control, while retention remains high across vulnerability classes. No case-level loss in the reference configuration is attributed to agent refusal or input normalization, and in one case the agent completed an attack by supplying calls the attacker omitted. Across the tested configurations, interface design affects exploitability more than agent choice, moving retention from 39% to 95% against at most 4.5 points across agents, but some restrictive interfaces also limit legitimate workflows. Our study provides a systematic empirical account of how agent-mediated access reshapes existing Web vulnerabilities, grounding future Web architecture design in measured security outcomes and trade-offs between reducing attack exposure and preserving legitimate functionality in agent-facing services.
item.dc:creator: Ruozhao Yang, Jiongchi Yu, Ming Hu, Xiaofei Xie

item.title: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.35624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An adversary brain is an LLM-based model of a threat actor's behavior, held as an evolving logical signature: a hypothesis with enough structure that data can test it continuously, without a person re-interpreting it each time. Rather than any single observation, such as an IoC (Indicator of Compromise), it is the arrangement that becomes a detection, or intelligence, mechanism. Where YARA matches a file and Sigma matches a log line, an adversary brain matches the activity pattern of a campaign or threat actor. This is based on an intelligence analysis technique called Analysis of Competing Hypotheses (ACH), which the design lifts from the limitation of a few hypotheses at a time, to thousands, and then also operationalizes it for continuous detection purposes. Language models make the concept, and scale, practical: they turn prose reports into brains, judge matches, and drive the loop that keeps brains current. A partial pattern in a brain can also match a new value, such as a fresh C2 (command and control) domain name, assisting with the discovery of new indicators, and turning unknown unknowns into known unknowns, and potentially into knowns. The author would like to thank Ryan Moon for the collaboration, and Sounil Yu, Chris Inglis, Thomas Roccia, Marius Benthin, Israel Grimberg, Michal Kamensky, Justin Borland, Brandon Levene, John Hultquist, and John Bambenek for their feedback and assistance.

item.title: A Category-Selective Encryption Framework for Privacy Protection of UAV Images
item.description: arXiv:2610.35729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems increasingly raises privacy concerns, as UAV aerial surveillance routinely captures sensitive objects such as pedestrians and vehicles alongside ordinary scene content. Existing privacy-preserving approaches typically employ class-agnostic saliency detection to indiscriminately obfuscate all visually salient regions, leading to unnecessary information loss and hindering downstream scene analysis. This paper proposes a category-selective encryption framework for privacy-preserving UAV surveillance. The core advance over prior class-agnostic approaches is semantic-level selectivity: the system first recognizes what is present in the scene via an 80-class detector, then encrypts only user-specified sensitive categories while leaving non-sensitive objects and background intact for downstream analytics. The framework supports two complementary encryption schemes: Thumbnail-Preserving Encryption (TPE), which applies adaptive pixelation with a learnable blend parameter and recovers content through a jointly trained Enhanced U-Net, and XOR stream cipher encryption, which offers parameter-free, mathematically exact reversibility. The architectural design, composite loss formulation, and joint training methodology are presented in detail, establishing a foundation for practical privacy-preserving UAV surveillance that balances protection strength and scene utility.
item.dc:creator: Ting Yan, Minghui Shang, Haolang Sun, Xu Wang, Yamin Han, Mingze He

item.title: Atomic Security Concerns: Towards a Foundational Language for Security Knowledge Representation
item.description: arXiv:2610.35782v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cybersecurity governance, risk management, compliance, and security architecture rely on numerous concepts, including security properties, domains, controls, risks, implementation measures, capabilities, and compliance requirements. Although these concepts are widely used, they are often represented through heterogeneous abstractions and vocabularies, making relationships among them difficult to express consistently and leaving much of the associated reasoning dependent on expert knowledge. This paper introduces the concepts of Security Concerns and Atomic Security Concerns (ASCs) and explores the hypothesis that cybersecurity knowledge may be represented through a finite set of foundational concerns. Inspired by the role of atoms in chemistry, the proposed approach views cybersecurity concepts as compositions of more fundamental concerns rather than as independent abstractions. Hence, Atomic Security Concerns could be viewed as a common abstraction layer for the representation of cybersecurity concepts, independently of their domain, nature, or level of granularity. Building upon this perspective, the paper explores how Atomic Security Concerns may provide the vocabulary of a cybersecurity language and how cybersecurity concepts may be represented as concern sets supporting explicit relationships among concepts. The contribution of this work is intentionally conceptual: it introduces a framework and research hypothesis for investigating the foundations of a common language for cybersecurity knowledge representation, reasoning, and future formalization.
item.dc:creator: Hanane Houmani

item.title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.35829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A vulnerability costs more to fix the later it is discovered. As coding agents generate code faster than developers can review it, software needs a first line of defense screening each new function in real time. LLM agents have recently become capable of finding real-world vulnerabilities by working as a security expert would: they run analysis tools, explore the surrounding code, test hypotheses and weigh the evidence before forming their own judgement. This reasoning, however, spans many model calls, so that each verdict takes minutes of compute, far too long for real-time screening. Faster detectors, which fine-tune deep learning models or prompt an LLM for a direct verdict, are less accurate: they judge a function without the context an agent gathers, and an LLM's generated verdict is unreliable even when given some of it. We present REVA (REal-time Vulnerability Analysis), an AI vulnerability detector that brings the security context and code understanding components behind agentic detectors into a single forward pass of an LLM. For each new function, REVA gives the LLM a pre-computed threat model of its module, lightweight static analysis findings and call-graph information. REVA leverages a trained probe to read the LLM's internal representations of the new function in this context. On PrimeVul's held-out test set, REVA on GLM-5.3-Flash reaches 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function. This matches VulTriage (59.2%), the state-of-the-art agentic detector, run on the same LLM, while being over 250 times faster and less than a tenth as costly. On the same prompt, the probe is 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict. Across three open LLMs, REVA is at least as accurate as VulTriage, and about 10% more accurate on two of them. An LLM's internal representations thus encode much of what agentic detectors obtain through reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Amine Lbath, Massih-Reza Amini

item.title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
item.description: arXiv:2610.35835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Breckenridge, Dani Vilardell, Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Ari Juels

item.title: ToolContractGate: Versioned Trusted Contracts for Drift-Safe Agent Tool Invocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33108v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent tool approval and input validation do not, by themselves, bind a request to an approved source artifact. ToolContractGate provides a deterministic runtime contract evaluator for OpenAPI-derived agent tools. Each versioned ToolContract combines a stored OpenAPI fingerprint with access, schema, and behavioral declarations. The full evaluator applies ten checks, including a cached boot-time provenance result; four execution modes and five evaluation configurations support baseline, ablation, and non-blocking shadow analysis. On a synthetic benchmark of 45 cases (35 unsafe cases across 12 drift classes and 10 safe cases), the full pipeline detects all 35 faults: 29 BLOCK, 3 REVIEW, and 3 WARN decisions, with no false blocks on the safe cases. The archived run reports a mean gate latency of 0.18 ms and a 95th percentile (p95) of 2 ms using integer-millisecond measurements. The open-source artifact includes seven OpenAPI specifications, twelve enterprise contracts, 29 unit tests, and a 900-record evaluation. Results characterize contract-decision coverage; downstream enforcement requires a host that honors the returned decision. Production traffic, semantic backend drift, and dynamic provenance refresh remain evaluation and integration opportunities.
item.dc:creator: Sachin Gupta

item.title: Post-Quantum Perfect Zero-Knowledge Arguments for NP From Any One-Way Permutation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we show for the first time that post-quantum one-way permutations are sufficient for perfect zero-knowledge classical arguments for all of NP with security guaranteed against quantum adversaries. We first establish that Naor, Ostrovsky,Venkatesen, and Yung's bit commitment scheme built from any permutation using interactive hashing, called the NOVY scheme, is sum-binding and collapse-binding against quantum polynomial-time committers provided the permutation is post-quantum one-way. We then show that the collapse-binding property of the NOVY scheme allows for Blum's perfect zero-knowledge argument for HAMCYCLE to remain so exactly as it stands against quantum adversaries.
item.dc:creator: Fr\'ed\'eric Dupuis, R\'emi Ligez, Khaireddine Medhioub, Louis Salvail, Louis-Charles Thibodeau

item.title: Bounds on polynomial approximations of the discrete logarithm function
item.description: arXiv:2610.33452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We revisit a classical result of Coppersmith and Shparlinski showing bounds on how well polynomials can approximate the discrete log function. They showed that for any univariate polynomial $f(X) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X]$ with $deg(f) \leq D$, we have: $$ |\{ x \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times \mid f(x) = dlog(x) \}| \leq \sqrt{2 D p}.$$ We show two improvements: (1) For all $D$, we improve the upper bound above to $(1+o(1)) \cdot \sqrt{Dp}$. In particular, we give nontrivial upper bounds on the approximation even for $D > p/2$. This new upper bound is the Johnson bound from the theory of list-decoding of error-correcting codes, and in fact our proof uses a connection to that problem, as well as other combinatorial ideas. (2) For $D = 1$, where both the above bounds are $O(\sqrt{p})$, we give an asymptotically improved upper bound of $O(p^{2/5})$. This is based on the sum-product phenomenon of additive combinatorics. We also improve the [CS00] bounds on the number of points of the form $(x, dlog(x)) \in \mathbb{F}_p^2$ that any bivariate polynomial $Q(X,Y) \in \mathbb{F}_p[X,Y]$ with $deg(Q) \leq D$ can vanish on, with our new bounds approaching the analogue of the Johnson bound for this problem.
item.dc:creator: Swastik Kopparty, Rishabh Kothary, Ashutosh Shankar

item.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?
item.description: arXiv:2610.33509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
item.dc:creator: Yihan Yang, Chenyuan Yang, Zijie Zhao, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Ziqi Zhang, Weidong Wang, Zhiheng Lyu, Lingming Zhang

item.title: Extraction meets Distillation - cryptanalytic techniques to recover parameters from a Deep Neural Network
item.description: arXiv:2610.33671v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study fully connected neural-network reconstruction by combining cryptanalytic weight-direction extraction with learning from predicted labels. We adapt a ReLU extraction implementation to Leaky ReLU, compare sign-search methods, and estimate biases and output layers. We prove conditional bounds for direction recovery with approximate prefixes, preservation of local distance votes, prediction changes from aligned parameter errors, and sign selection with independent scoring data. We also specify exact row restoration and distinguish its guarantee from that of gradient masking. The experiments evaluate assisted extraction, with privileged access to gradients, hidden activations, and victim parameters, followed by label-based reconstruction. Across eight search seeds on the largest synthetic architecture, Leaky ReLU recovers 51--57 neurons in the deepest hidden layer, while ReLU recovers none. This advantage does not hold uniformly across architectures and layers. Removing victim-weight access from the sign walk gives less accurate signs, despite high final prediction agreement. Across 40 seeded runs on the two smallest synthetic victims, agreement on 5,000 inputs excluded from fitting and selection ranges from $0.9890$ to $0.9992$. On two CIFAR-10 victims, the reconstructed models achieve $56.40\%$ and $58.29\%$ agreement and exceed the distillation baseline on three functional metrics. We report label requests separately from privileged access and explain why prediction agreement does not identify network parameters.
item.dc:creator: Biprarshi Biswas, Arya Anshuman Ojha, Yubaraj Das, Devansh Khosla, Kamran Rais, Saankhya Samanta, Subhamoy Maitra, Pantelimon Stanica

item.title: A Rowhammer attack on Fil-C's software capabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.33748v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Rowhammer is a hardware vulnerability in dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) in which repeated accesses to one or more aggressor rows can induce bit-flips in nearby victim rows. This phenomenon violates a core assumption of conventional programming language semantics: that reading from or writing to one memory location does not modify others. Despite the security importance of this phenomenon, there is no widely established formal framework connecting Rowhammer faults with program behaviour. This makes it difficult to reason rigorously about the efficacy of proposed Rowhammer defences and the program-level guarantees they provide. To address this gap, we present a probabilistic small-step operational semantics for an idealised imperative language subject to Rowhammer-style faults. The semantics is high-level in that it abstracts from DRAM internals and semiconductor physics. A general probabilistic fault model parameterises the semantics, representing Rowhammer-style faults by assigning probabilities to bit-flips during read or write operations within a specified victim region. The resulting distributions are propagated through programs using the standard monadic structure of probabilistic computation. As a case study, we formalise physical separation, a well-known defence that places program variables sufficiently far apart in physical memory that an access to one variable cannot disturb another. We prove a distribution-independent semantic collapse theorem: for every finite execution, including prefixes of terminating and non-terminating executions, the protected projection of the probabilistic Rowhammer semantics is the Dirac distribution of the corresponding Rowhammer-free execution. Furthermore, we develop an observation-parametric account of secure information flow.
item.dc:creator: Amir Naseredini, Suhas Viswanath, Martin Berger

item.title: EdgeDeID: A 0.6B Clinical De-identifier Trained Without Real Patient Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.33839v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: De-identifying clinical notes with a hosted language model discloses the information the step is meant to protect. We present EdgeDeID, a 0.6B-parameter decoder-only de-identifier that runs locally and is trained without real patient text: three LLM teachers write synthetic notes, a single labeler re-annotates them into one convention, and the model learns to emit a typed XML schema of the identifiers it finds. On a 100-note synthetic in-domain benchmark with manually verified annotations it reaches 0.994 micro-F1 and leaves no missed identifier in 99% of notes, against 0.857 and 12% for the strongest of eight off-the-shelf systems. Quantized, it runs on CPU in 615 MB. Of three additions to supervised training, only a verifier adapter helps: it separates complete from incomplete outputs of other systems at 0.94 AUROC, whereas reinforcement learning with a recall-weighted reward and a rule-based post-processing layer leave in-domain results unchanged. On MIMIC ICU nursing notes F1 falls to 0.48. The errors follow two properties our synthetic notes lack, telegraphic style and low identifier density, and three hand-written in-context examples recover 0.08 F1 without annotated target data.
item.dc:creator: Sina Daneshgar, Raya Namazi, Amirali Khosravi, Pouria Rouzrokh, Bardia Khosravi

item.title: Reversible Pseudonymisation of Documents Sent to External LLMs: an Open Bilingual Benchmark and an Engine
item.description: arXiv:2610.34012v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Professionals send working documents to external large language models. A common safeguard is reversible pseudonymisation: personal data are replaced with placeholders before the request and restored locally in the answer. We present an open benchmark of five existing open tools and a regular-expression baseline on Russian and UK English, and an open engine built on the two strongest tools. The benchmark excludes each tool's own authors' dataset from its verdict, compares the engine with each tool on identical datasets for detection, reports masking precision, and tests on a held-out set of synthetic documents whose files, hashes, decision rules, run plan and stopping rule were published before any run. Two local LLMs test whether placeholders survive. All evaluation data are synthetic, and the benchmark was run by the author of the engine; code, data, predictions and raw answers are released. On external datasets no existing tool meets all predefined thresholds: in UK English the identifier and leak thresholds are not met, in Russian the identifier threshold is borderline. On the last held-out set of 1,000 documents per language, the best existing tools leave a whole value visible in 61% (Russian) and 58% (UK) of documents. On these documents, from the generator it was developed on, the engine does so in 0.3% [0.1; 0.9] and 0.2% [0.1; 0.7], leaves any part of a value visible in 0.8% and 0.2%, and meets all detection thresholds in both languages. In UK English it also restores at least 99% of its placeholders after 760 answers. In Russian it restores only 94.6% [93.6; 95.6] of name placeholders, against a 99% threshold, mainly because the inflection it borrows from pii-guard produces wrong surname forms. The engine was developed over six earlier held-out sets from the same generator; real documents were not tested.
item.dc:creator: Vladimir Beskorovainyi

item.title: Securing Agent-Generated Code with Its Own Development History
item.description: arXiv:2610.34098v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Pull requests written by coding agents can pass a project's test suite while omitting a guard or a validation step. To find the missing condition, a reviewer currently relies on static analysis of the final code. An agent-generated change, however, is accompanied by a development history that a human commit does not provide. The agent's trajectory records each edit together with the agent's stated assumptions, and structural differencing shows how each changed function evolved. We present TRACER, a workflow that uses this development history as evidence for security review. TRACER tracks changes at the symbol level, treats the agent's recorded rationale as claims to be verified against the current code, accepts a repair only after assessment and functional validation, and attaches to each accepted repair an executable check that later changes must satisfy. On the SusVibes benchmark, symbol-level tracking places the vulnerable symbol in the review scope for 94.6% of agent patches, compared with 13.4% for the primary scanner warning. With two investigator models, the configuration that includes the agent's rationale yields the largest number of verified security repairs while preserving functionality, and adding AST history to it does not increase that number. A funnel analysis identifies where the remaining candidates are lost. In a study of structural-biology software, the combination of repair memory and a boundary check allows a subsequent feature request to succeed in nine of ten tasks without reintroducing the repaired vulnerability, whereas functional feedback alone succeeds in four and reintroduces the vulnerability in three.

item.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics
item.description: arXiv:2610.34121v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning supports cooperative decision-making in Internet of Things systems, but strategic deviations can disrupt coordination and undermine confidence in the training process. This paper proposes Blockchain-Enabled Centralized Training and Decentralized Execution (BE-CTDE), which uses blockchain as an active training-management layer. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations; its flags drive a token mechanism combining slashing, burning, rewards, and compensation. Retained balances determine each agent's contribution to the global policy update, connecting auditable behavior to learning influence. We derive a one-round incentive condition that accounts for action-dependent compensation and the payoff from deviation, and a finite expected exclusion-time bound under explicit conditional detection and accounting assumptions, showing perfect detection is unnecessary. An exact finite-population capacity bound characterizes the limits of the population-relative detector. In multi-agent path finding experiments, BE-CTDE outperforms a state-of-the-art learning-based path planner with substantially higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries form the majority. It also outperforms partially defended baselines in all configurations, with collision rates up to 35% lower than under detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than under conventional stake slashing. Together, these results characterize how behavioral verification and token feedback can support accountable cooperative learning.
item.dc:creator: Chih-Wei Huang, Hsin-Chieh Lee, Yun-Chen Yu, Ibrahim Althamary, Rongxing Lu, Phone Lin

item.title: The Policies of Programming Language Ecosystems: A "Qualitative" Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.34187v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Programming language ecosystems (PLEs), such as CRAN for R, have greatly accelerated software reuse. At the same time, they have increased software supply-chain risks and incidents. However, the problems are not limited to cyber security; everything from illegal content and content moderation to harassment and sexual content are mentioned in many policies of popular PLEs. The paper examines these policies. According to a moderate agreement between the three authors on 38 distinct policy categories and eight PLE policies, the policies generally exhibit divergence rather than convergence. However, some policy categories, such as those about malware, intellectual property, and content removal, are universally recognized. The divergence is thus seen in more fine-grained policy categories, such as those related to package size limits, manipulation of metrics, typo-squatting, and binary uploads. These and other related qualitative results patch a notable gap in existing PLE research.
item.dc:creator: Jukka Ruohonen, Rahime Yilmaz, Krzysztof Sierszecki

item.title: Decentralized Medical Data Sharing with Off-chain Storage and View-based Access Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.34279v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recently, many blockchain-based medical data sharing systems using off-chain storage have been proposed. However, these systems have some drawbacks such as being incompletely decentralized, low adaptability to cloud storages, high cost, and low security. It is non-trivial to address the drawbacks due to the transparency, immutability, and decentralization of a blockchain platform. Our goal is to design a decentralized medical data sharing system with off-chain storage that addresses all the above drawbacks while satisfying data protection and privacy laws. We propose the VASCO (View-based AccesS COntrol) system that does not rely on any central server including a key generation one, not rely on any special cloud storage including IPFS, not use a secure channel, encrypts both data and metadata, and supports end-to-end encryption. We achieve it by designing eight chaincodes rigorously based on view-based access control. For a medical data ecosystem that consists of many stakeholders who employ different data standards, storage formats, and transmission protocols, we present how typical flows of medical data in the ecosystem can be achieved by using the proposed chaincodes with interoperability. We showed that VASCO is superior to the existing systems in terms of both functionality and regulatory compliance. We also tested the scalability of VASCO using a blockchain of 21 peer nodes with different specifications and verified interoperability through 30 combinations of standards, formats, and protocols. VASCO is a promising medical data sharing system that can provide secure and efficient sharing of medical data while preserving patient privacy and satisfying regulatory compliance with interoperability. The result of this study provides a potential to improve patient outcomes and advance medical research for the medical data ecosystem.
item.dc:creator: Hajin Jeon, Hyung-Jin Yoon, Jemin Lee, Min-Soo Kim

item.title: Factual Yet One-Sided: Stance Poisoning and Evidence Balancing in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.34294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The stance expressed in responses from retrieval-augmented generation systems is significantly influenced by the stance distribution of the retrieved materials. Existing research on knowledge poisoning has primarily targeted factual errors. In contrast, this study focuses on injection attacks in which the facts are correct but the stance on a controversial issue is one-sided. At a mean topic-level poisoning share of 18.9% within the post-injection ProCon documents, all four generation models from different vendors exhibited stance shifts aligned with the poisoning direction; across four concentration levels, the shifts increased monotonically. This paper proposes a Stance-Balancing Middleware positioned between the retriever and the generator. It consists of stance detection, fixed balancing (2 supporting + 2 opposing + 1 neutral), and a debiasing prompt, without introducing additional large language model calls. Across all eight concentration-direction settings, the complete method reduced the magnitude of stance deviation by an estimated 0.106 to 0.350; the six settings at poisoning shares of 11.9%-18.9% remained significant after Holm adjustment (adjusted p <= 0.009). In the cross-model experiment, all eight model-direction combinations moved along the stance axis in the corrective direction, and seven of eight showed a clearly detected reduction in absolute distance from 0. In the concentration sweep, the post-defense intervals included 0 in all eight settings, while the cross-model pro-poisoning results retained small positive residual point estimates of +0.045 to +0.063. For 20 candidate documents, stance detection took approximately 1.5% of the median generation time on a single GPU and approximately 16% on CPU.
item.dc:creator: Puyuan Yang, Shaoxuan Dong, Liujie Wu, Xiaochun Cheng, Bo Li

item.title: SymLift: Neural Semantic Lifting for Compile-Free Vulnerability Detection in Context-Incomplete Code Fragments
item.description: arXiv:2610.34431v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Missing project context can prevent build-dependent analyzers from constructing program relations required for vulnerability detection, while neural predictions alone do not establish auditable derivations. We present SymLift, a compile-free framework centered on Vulnerability-Oriented Neural Semantic Lifting for context-incomplete code fragments. A fine-tuned large language model reconstructs vulnerability-relevant control-flow, data-flow, memory, and resource relations in a constrained LLVM-like intermediate representation (IR), without reconstructing the full project context or directly predicting vulnerability labels. A deterministic parser validates the IR and maps its supported operations and relations into normalized evidence facts. Explicit Datalog rules derive findings with supporting facts and derivation traces, ensuring deterministic reasoning for fixed facts and rules. We evaluate SymLift on FormAI, Juliet, and MegaVul. Reducing complete Juliet programs to function-level fragments lowers Clang compilation success from 100% to 12.00%, whereas SymLift's analysis completion rate decreases by only 1.17 percentage points. After task-specific fine-tuning, the lifter achieves a control-flow intersection over union (IoU) of 96.85% on FormAI. SymLift-Qwen-7B achieves a Target-F1 of 94.41% on FormAI and, across six vulnerability families on MegaVul, a micro-averaged precision of 98.24% and a micro-averaged Target-F1 of 91.66%. These results support accurate and auditable detection in the evaluated context-incomplete settings, even with partial program relations.
